pages.title: SOLID PRINCIPLES CHEAT SHEET
pages.subtitle: Five rules for code that bends without breaking
pages.learner: Why does fixing one thing break three?

panels.heading: What SOLID Means
panels.body:
SOLID = five object-oriented design rules.
S: single responsibility. O: open/closed.
L: Liskov substitution. I: interface segregation.
D: dependency inversion.
Goal: changes stay small, local and safe.
panels.diagram: Five glowing letter blocks S-O-L-I-D forming a foundation, each block labeled with its full name; a sturdy wall labeled 'features' stands on top while a cracked wall labeled 'spaghetti' leans beside it.

panels.heading: S - Single Responsibility
panels.body:
A class should have one reason to change.
Before: Report computes totals AND writes PDFs.
After: Report computes; PdfExporter writes.
Test: describe the class without saying "and".
panels.code:
class Report: ...       # totals only
class PdfExporter: ...  # output only
panels.diagram: Before/after split: one overloaded box 'Report: totals + PDF' with two red arrows labeled 'finance change' and 'layout change'; after, two boxes 'Report' and 'PdfExporter', each with a single arrow.

panels.heading: O - Open/Closed
panels.body:
Open for extension, closed for modification.
Before: an if/elif chain on payment kind grows forever.
After: each payment type is a class with pay().
Add features by adding code, not editing it.
panels.code:
for method in methods:
    method.pay(amount)  # no if/elif
panels.diagram: Left: a long if/elif ladder 'card / paypal / crypto / ...' with a red 'edit again' stamp. Right: a socket labeled 'pay()' with plug-in cards Card, Wallet, Crypto snapping in.

panels.heading: L - Liskov Substitution
panels.body:
Subtypes must work wherever the base type works.
Classic break: Square(Rectangle) - setting width silently changes height.
No stronger preconditions, no weaker guarantees, no surprise exceptions.
panels.diagram: A function 'resize(rect)' expecting area 20 (w=4, h=5); a Rectangle passes with green check, a Square plugged in yields area 25 with a red X and the label 'broke the contract'.

panels.heading: I - Interface Segregation
panels.body:
Clients should not depend on methods they never use.
Before: one Machine with print(), scan(), fax().
After: small Printer and Scanner protocols.
A basic printer no longer fakes fax().
panels.diagram: Before: a fat 'Machine' remote with three buttons, a cheap printer forced to wire a dummy 'fax' button (red). After: two slim remotes 'Printer' and 'Scanner'.

panels.heading: D - Dependency Inversion
panels.body:
High-level code depends on abstractions, not details.
Before: OrderService builds MySQLRepo() inside.
After: it receives any repo with save().
Tests swap in a fake repo in one line.
panels.diagram: Arrow diagram: before, OrderService -> MySQLRepo (hard arrow, red). After, OrderService -> 'Repo interface: save()' <- MySQLRepo and FakeRepo both pointing up to the interface.

panels.heading: Pitfalls: When to Bend
panels.body:
SOLID is a guide, not a law.
Over-splitting: 40 one-method classes for a 50-line script.
Premature abstraction: an interface with one implementation forever.
Bend for prototypes and scripts; refactor when change hurts.
panels.diagram: Warning panel in orange: a tiny script exploded into a swarm of 40 micro-boxes connected by tangled arrows, labeled 'over-engineered'; a balance scale weighing 'simplicity' vs 'flexibility'.

panels.heading: Check Yourself
panels.body:
Bird has fly(). Penguin(Bird) raises an error in fly().
Which principle breaks?
Answer: L - split into Bird and FlyingBird.
panels.diagram: Quiz card: a penguin standing on a 'Bird' pedestal with a red error bubble 'cannot fly'; revealed answer tab shows a tree Bird -> FlyingBird -> Eagle, and Bird -> Penguin.

pages.footer: Small, focused pieces that depend on promises, not details.
pages.summary: Explains the five SOLID object-oriented design principles with tiny before/after Python examples, and when it is sensible to bend them.

pages.title: CREATIONAL PATTERNS CHEAT SHEET
pages.subtitle: Control how objects get made

panels.heading: Why Creational Patterns
panels.body:
They separate creating an object from using it.
Callers ask for what they need, not how to build it.
Five classics from the Gang of Four (GoF) book.
panels.diagram: A factory conveyor: raw parts enter a machine labeled 'creation', finished objects exit to a 'client' who only sees the product; five machine doors labeled Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype.

panels.heading: Singleton (Often an Anti-Pattern)
panels.body:
Problem: exactly one shared instance (config, logger).
Risks: hidden global state, tests leak into each other.
A Python module is already a singleton.
Prefer: create one object and inject it.
panels.diagram: One glowing object in the center with many classes reaching for it via tangled red wires labeled 'hidden dependency'; side note shows the cleaner version: main() creates Config once and hands it down with arrows.

panels.heading: Factory Method
panels.body:
Problem: the caller should not hard-code which class to build.
A method creates the object; subclasses override it.
Use when the type depends on context or config.
panels.diagram: Class diagram: Exporter.make_writer() -> CsvWriter; subclass JsonExporter overrides make_writer() -> JsonWriter; the shared export() method calls make_writer() without knowing the type.

panels.heading: Abstract Factory
panels.body:
Problem: families of objects that must match.
DarkTheme makes DarkButton + DarkMenu; LightTheme makes the light pair.
Swap the factory, every part changes together.
panels.code:
ui = DarkTheme()
button, menu = ui.button(), ui.menu()
panels.diagram: Two factory machines side by side: 'DarkTheme' producing a dark button and dark menu, 'LightTheme' producing light ones; a red X over a mixed dark-button/light-menu pair labeled 'mismatch prevented'.

panels.heading: Builder
panels.body:
Problem: many optional parts or steps.
Set parts step by step, then build() validates.
Avoids 10-argument constructors.
In Python, keyword arguments or dataclasses often suffice.
panels.code:
req = (RequestBuilder("GET", "/users")
       .header("Auth", token)
       .timeout(5)
       .build())
panels.diagram: Assembly line building an HTTP request: blocks 'GET /users' -> 'header Auth' -> 'timeout 5s' -> 'build()' stamp with a green check; beside it a crossed-out constructor with ten positional arguments.

panels.heading: Prototype
panels.body:
Problem: building from scratch is slow or complex.
Copy a configured template, then tweak the copy.
Shallow copies share nested lists - use deepcopy.
panels.code:
enemy = copy.deepcopy(base_enemy)
enemy.hp = 50
panels.diagram: A template enemy robot with stats (hp 100, items list) cloned via a copy beam into two copies; one copy edited to hp 50; a red callout shows a shallow copy whose shared 'items' list changes in both.

panels.heading: Which One When?
panels.body:
One shared resource -> inject one instance.
Type chosen at runtime -> Factory Method.
Matching families -> Abstract Factory.
Many optional settings -> Builder.
Cheap clones of a template -> Prototype.
panels.diagram: Decision flowchart with diamond questions 'need one instance?', 'type varies?', 'families must match?', 'many options?', 'copy a template?' each leading to a colored pattern badge.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Factories for classes that never vary are noise.
Singletons leak state between tests.
Builders that skip validation build broken objects.
Start with a plain constructor; add a pattern when pain appears.
panels.diagram: Orange warning board with three icons: an empty factory producing one identical box forever, two test tubes sharing one contaminated global, and a half-assembled robot leaving a builder without inspection.

pages.footer: Make creation a decision in one place, not a habit everywhere.
pages.summary: Covers the five Gang of Four creational patterns (Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype): the problem each solves, a short Python sketch, and when to use or avoid them.

pages.title: STRUCTURAL PATTERNS CHEAT SHEET
pages.subtitle: Compose objects into bigger, cleaner structures
pages.learner: How do I plug old code in?

panels.heading: What Structural Patterns Do
panels.body:
They connect classes and objects into larger structures.
Most are wrappers: an object holds another and forwards calls.
Same shape, different intent - learn the intent.
panels.diagram: Six puzzle pieces labeled Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy, Composite, Bridge snapping into one larger structure; a small inset shows a generic wrapper box holding an inner object with a forwarding arrow.

panels.heading: Adapter
panels.body:
Problem: a useful class has the wrong interface.
Your code calls pay(cents); the vendor SDK offers charge(dollars).
The adapter translates. Interface changes, behavior stays.
panels.diagram: A travel plug adapter: left socket labeled 'pay(cents)' (your code), right plug labeled 'charge(dollars)' (vendor SDK), the adapter in between converting 1999 cents -> 19.99 dollars.

panels.heading: Decorator
panels.body:
Problem: add behavior without a subclass per combination.
Wrap an object with the same interface plus extra work: logging, caching, retries.
Stack them: Retry(Cache(Api())).
panels.diagram: Russian-doll layers: innermost 'Api', wrapped by 'Cache', wrapped by 'Retry'; a call arrow travels inward and the result travels back out, each layer adding a small label.

panels.heading: Facade
panels.body:
Problem: a subsystem has too many parts to call correctly.
A facade offers one simple entry point.
Example: checkout() runs stock, payment, shipping and email in order.
panels.diagram: A clean storefront door labeled 'checkout()' in front of a messy back room with four machines: Stock, Payment, Shipping, Email, connected in sequence by numbered arrows.

panels.heading: Proxy
panels.body:
Problem: control access to a real object.
Same interface plus a gatekeeper step.
Kinds: virtual (lazy load), protection (auth check), remote (network stub), caching.
Example: ImageProxy loads the file on first display().
panels.diagram: A guard robot standing in front of a vault labeled 'RealImage (20 MB)'; client calls display() on the guard, which loads the image only on the first call; second call served instantly.

panels.heading: Composite
panels.body:
Problem: treat single items and groups the same way.
A tree where leaves and branches share one interface.
File.size() returns bytes; Folder.size() sums its children.
panels.diagram: Folder tree: 'docs/' contains 'a.txt 2 KB', 'b.png 5 KB' and 'img/' with 'c.jpg 3 KB'; sizes bubble up: img/ = 3 KB, docs/ = 10 KB.

panels.heading: Bridge
panels.body:
Problem: two dimensions of variation explode into subclasses.
Shapes x renderers: 3 x 2 = 6 classes.
Bridge: Shape holds a Renderer -> 3 + 2 = 5 classes.
Both sides vary independently.
panels.diagram: Left: a 3x2 grid of six classes (CircleSvg, CirclePng, ...) in red. Right: three shapes on one side, two renderers on the other, joined by a single bridge labeled 'has-a renderer'.

panels.heading: Compare + Pitfalls
panels.body:
Adapter changes the interface. Decorator adds behavior.
Proxy controls access. Facade simplifies many parts.
Pitfall: six wrapper layers make stack traces painful.
Pitfall: a facade that grows into a god object.
panels.diagram: Comparison table with four rows and intent icons (plug, onion layers, guard, storefront); orange warning strip below showing a deep wrapper tower and a bloated facade blob.

pages.footer: Wrap to adapt, add, guard or simplify - and name the intent.
pages.summary: Explains six structural design patterns (Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy, Composite, Bridge) with Python sketches, and how to tell look-alike wrappers apart by intent.

pages.title: BEHAVIORAL PATTERNS CHEAT SHEET
pages.subtitle: Who does what, and how objects talk
pages.learner: How do I kill this giant if/elif?

panels.heading: Strategy
panels.body:
Problem: swap an algorithm at runtime.
Pass the behavior in as an object or function.
Example: shipping is free over 50, else 5.
Cart of 40 -> total 45.
panels.diagram: A slot machine labeled 'checkout' with interchangeable cartridges 'standard', 'express', 'free over 50'; the 'free over 50' cartridge inserted, with total 40 + 5 = 45 on the display.

panels.heading: Observer
panels.body:
Problem: many objects react when one changes.
The subject keeps a list of subscribers and notifies each on events.
Used in UIs, event buses, pub/sub.
panels.code:
for callback in self.subscribers:
    callback(event)
panels.diagram: A broadcast tower labeled 'Subject: price changed' sending signal waves to three listeners: Chart, Alert, Logger, each with a subscribe arrow back to the tower.

panels.heading: Command
panels.body:
Problem: treat a request as an object.
A command packs action + data with execute() and undo().
Enables queues, logs, retries and undo/redo.
panels.code:
cmd = AddText(doc, "hi")
cmd.execute(); history.append(cmd)
history.pop().undo()
panels.diagram: A stack of command cards 'AddText "hi"', 'Bold', 'Delete' piled in a history tray; an undo arrow pops the top card and reverses it.

panels.heading: State
panels.body:
Problem: behavior depends on the current state.
Each state is a class; the object delegates to it.
Order: Pending -> Paid -> Shipped.
ship() while Pending raises an error - no 6-way if.
panels.diagram: State machine with three nodes Pending, Paid, Shipped joined by arrows 'pay()' and 'ship()'; a red blocked arrow from Pending straight to Shipped labeled 'invalid'.

panels.heading: Template Method
panels.body:
Problem: same steps, a few details differ.
The base class fixes the skeleton; subclasses fill in hooks.
export() = load -> format -> save; CSV and JSON override only format().
panels.diagram: Three-step rail 'load -> format -> save' with the middle step as a swappable slot; CSV and JSON cartridges hovering above the slot.

panels.heading: Iterator
panels.body:
Problem: walk a collection without exposing its internals.
Python builds it in: __iter__ / __next__, or a generator with yield.
Works for trees, files, paginated APIs.
panels.diagram: A conveyor belt pulling items one by one out of a closed box labeled 'paginated API (pages 1..3)'; a for-loop robot takes each item as it arrives.

panels.heading: Chain of Responsibility
panels.body:
Problem: several handlers might process a request.
Pass it along a chain; each link handles, stops or forwards.
Example: web middleware auth -> rate limit -> validate -> handler.
panels.diagram: A request envelope moving through four gates: Auth (pass), Rate limit (pass), Validate (pass), Handler (done); an alternate red path shows the envelope stopped at Auth with '401'.

panels.heading: Compare + Pitfalls
panels.body:
Strategy: the caller picks behavior. State: the object switches itself.
Template Method uses inheritance; Strategy uses composition.
Pitfall: a one-method class where a function would do.
Pitfall: observer cascades hide control flow.
panels.diagram: Side-by-side mini diagrams Strategy vs State and Template Method vs Strategy; orange warning strip showing a tangled web of observers triggering each other in a loop.

pages.footer: Name the behavior, give it an object, and swap it freely.
pages.summary: Covers seven behavioral design patterns (Strategy, Observer, Command, State, Template Method, Iterator, Chain of Responsibility) with short Python sketches and how to choose between similar ones.

pages.title: CLEAN CODE & REFACTORING
pages.subtitle: Write for the next reader - often future you
pages.learner: Who wrote this mess? Oh... me.

panels.heading: Naming
panels.body:
Names reveal intent.
Bad: d, data2, process(). Good: days_overdue, send_invoice().
Booleans read as questions: is_active, has_access.
One word per concept: not fetch, get and retrieve.
panels.diagram: Two name tags side by side: red tag 'd = 7' with a confused reader, green tag 'days_overdue = 7' with a nodding reader; small chips 'is_active', 'has_access' below.

panels.heading: Small Functions
panels.body:
One function = one job at one level of detail.
Few parameters (3 or fewer is a good default).
No hidden side effects: validate() should not save.
panels.code:
def place_order(cart):
    validate(cart)
    charge(cart.total)
    send_receipt(cart)
panels.diagram: A 200-line monster function split into four small labeled blocks: validate, charge, send_receipt, all called in order from a short place_order().

panels.heading: DRY, KISS, YAGNI
panels.body:
DRY = don't repeat yourself: one source of truth per rule.
KISS = keep it simple: simplest thing that works.
YAGNI = you aren't gonna need it: no code for imagined futures.
Rule of three: abstract on the third copy.
panels.diagram: Three badges: DRY (one master copy feeding three users), KISS (straight arrow beating a maze), YAGNI (crossed-out 'future plugin system' blueprint); a counter showing copy 1, 2, 3 -> extract.

panels.heading: Composition Over Inheritance
panels.body:
Inheritance = "is-a", tightly coupled to the parent.
Composition = "has-a": build from swappable parts.
Before: a LoggingRetryingCachedClient subclass chain.
After: Client(cache=..., retry=..., logger=...).
panels.diagram: Left: a tall fragile tower of subclasses Client -> CachedClient -> RetryingCachedClient -> LoggingRetryingCachedClient. Right: one Client box with three plug-in modules Cache, Retry, Logger.

panels.heading: Dependency Injection
panels.body:
DI = pass dependencies in instead of creating them inside.
Code becomes testable and swappable.
Inject a fake clock -> deterministic output.
panels.diagram: A function box with an input port labeled 'clock'; in production a real wall clock plugs in, in tests a frozen clock showing 09:00 plugs in and the output reads 'Good morning'.

panels.heading: Code Smells -> Refactoring Moves
panels.body:
Long function -> Extract Function.
Duplicate code -> extract and reuse.
Long parameter list -> Introduce Parameter Object.
Type switch everywhere -> Replace Conditional with Polymorphism.
Magic number 86400 -> SECONDS_PER_DAY.
panels.diagram: Two-column table: left column smells with stink-cloud icons, right column refactoring moves with wrench icons, arrows connecting each row.

panels.heading: Refactor Safely With Tests
panels.body:
Refactoring = change structure, not behavior.
1. Tests green first (pin legacy behavior with characterization tests).
2. One tiny step. 3. Run tests. 4. Commit.
Never mix refactoring and new features in one commit.
panels.diagram: A loop diagram: green test light -> tiny change -> run tests -> commit -> back to start; a red light branch says 'revert the last step'.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Big-bang rewrites stall for months; refactor in small steps.
Over-DRY: merging look-alike code that changes for different reasons.
Clever one-liners hurt readability.
Comments should explain why, not what.
panels.diagram: Orange warning board: a crumbling 'rewrite from scratch' tower, two different gears forced into one shared gear and jamming, a tangled one-liner knot.

pages.footer: Clean code is a habit: clear names, small steps, green tests.
pages.summary: Teaches everyday clean-code habits (naming, small functions, DRY/KISS/YAGNI, composition over inheritance, dependency injection) and how to map code smells to safe, test-backed refactoring moves.
